title: The Quantitative Follow-Up to Fishburn's Theorem
content: After Fishburn (1995) proved ∑f(u)² = O(n³) for convex polygons, the natural question is: what is the exact constant? The regular n-gon achieves Θ(n³), and analysis of its distance structure suggests the asymptotic constant is 1/2. The file formalizes this constant question and connects it to the Erdős-Fishburn extremality conjecture. Unlike the original Erdős #94 (which asked for the O(n³) bound), this open question OQ-02 asks for the precise coefficient.
mathContext: The squared-multiplicity sum is $S(P) = \sum_u f(u)^2$ where $f(u)$ counts the number of pairs $\{p, q\} \subseteq P$ with $|p - q| = u$. Fishburn proved $S(P) \leq C \cdot n^3$ for convex $n$-gons. The question is whether $S(\text{reg}_n) / n^3 \to c$ and what $c$ is. The heuristic: $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ distinct distances, most with multiplicity $n$, gives $\sum f^2 \approx (n/2) \cdot n^2 = n^3/2$, suggesting $c = 1/2$.

title: Core Definitions: Point Configurations and the S Function
content: `Point` is aliased to `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)` — the 2D Euclidean plane in Mathlib. `PointConfig` is a `Finset Point`, a finite set of plane points. `InConvexPosition P` is defined as: no point of P lies in the convex hull of the remaining points. This is the standard definition of strict convex position (vertices of a convex polygon). The crucial axiom `S : PointConfig → ℕ` declares the squared-multiplicity sum as an axiomatized function — its exact formula is not given in Lean; only the key properties are axiomatized.
mathContext: $\text{Point} = \mathbb{R}^2$ (as `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)`). A configuration $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ is in convex position iff $\forall p \in P,\; p \notin \text{conv}(P \setminus \{p\})$. The squared-multiplicity sum: $S(P) = \sum_{u > 0} |\{\{p, q\} \subseteq P : |pq| = u\}|^2$. Equivalently, $S(P) = \sum_{i \neq j} |\{(a, b) : |ab| = |p_ip_j|\}|$. The axiom `S : PointConfig → ℕ` says this function exists and maps to natural numbers.

title: Regular n-gon and Asymptotic Constant via Classical Choice
content: `regularNGon n` constructs the regular n-gon inscribed in the unit circle using `Finset.range n` and the parametrization (cos(2πk/n), sin(2πk/n)) for k = 0, ..., n-1. `S_regular n = S (regularNGon n)` is the squared-multiplicity sum for this configuration. The asymptotic constant is defined non-constructively via `Axiom.choose`: `asymptotic_constant_exists` axiomatizes the existence of a limit `c > 0` with `normalizedSum → c`, and `asymptoticConstant` is obtained via `choose`. This is a classic use of classical logic in Lean: the constant exists by axiom, and `choose` extracts it.
mathContext: The regular $n$-gon: $\text{reg}_n = \{(\cos(2\pi k/n), \sin(2\pi k/n)) : k = 0, \ldots, n-1\}$, inscribed in the unit circle. $\text{normalizedSum}(n) = S(\text{reg}_n) / n^3$. The axiom `asymptotic_constant_exists` asserts $\exists c > 0,\; \text{normalizedSum} \to c$ (Filter.Tendsto in nhds $c$). Then `asymptoticConstant = (asymptotic_constant_exists).choose` and `normalized_sum_converges : Filter.Tendsto normalizedSum atTop (nhds asymptoticConstant)` follows from `.choose_spec.2`.
relatedConcepts: regular polygon inscribed in unit circle

title: Why c = 1/2: The Regular n-gon Distance Structure
content: For a regular n-gon, there are ⌊n/2⌋ distinct distances d₁, ..., d_{⌊n/2⌋}. For k < n/2, the multiplicity of d_k is n (each vertex has exactly one pair at distance d_k in each direction). Only the diameter (when n is even) has multiplicity n/2. So ∑f(d_k)² ≈ ⌊n/2⌋·n² ≈ n³/2, giving c = 1/2. The theorem `dominant_contribution` makes this rigorous: ⌊n/2⌋·n² ≥ n³/2 - n², so the S_regular lower bound is at least n³/2 - n² for n ≥ 3. The proof uses `Nat.div_mul_le_self` and `Nat.lt_div_mul_add` to bound ⌊n/2⌋ in terms of (n-1)/2.
mathContext: The distinct distances in $\text{reg}_n$ are $d_k = 2\sin(\pi k/n)$ for $k = 1, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. The multiplicity of $d_k$ is $n$ (for $k < n/2$) or $n/2$ (for $k = n/2$, only when $n$ even). So $S(\text{reg}_n) = \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - [n \text{ even}]} n^2 + [n \text{ even}] \cdot (n/2)^2 \approx \lfloor n/2 \rfloor \cdot n^2 \approx n^3/2$. The theorem proves: $(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor : \mathbb{R}) \cdot n^2 \geq n^3/2 - n^2$, using the bound $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor \geq (n-1)/2$.

title: Erdős-Fishburn Bridge: Extremality Implies Sharp Universal Bound
content: The Erdős-Fishburn conjecture asserts the regular n-gon maximizes ∑f(u)² among convex n-gons for large enough n. If true, and if c = 1/2, then S(P) ≤ (1/2 + ε)·n³ for ALL large convex polygons P. The theorem `erdos_fishburn_implies_universal_bound` proves the purely logical implication: Erdős-Fishburn (as a Prop) implies the Nat.cast version. `optimal_bound_from_conjecture` would combine both to get the (1/2+ε) bound — but this theorem has a `sorry` because the convergence argument requires additional work. `constant_ge_half` similarly has a sorry for the limit lower bound.
mathContext: Erdős-Fishburn: $\exists N,\; \forall n \geq N,\; \forall P \text{ convex},\; |P|=n \Rightarrow S(P) \leq S(\text{reg}_n)$. Combined with $c = 1/2$: for any $\varepsilon > 0$, $\exists N$ such that $n \geq N \Rightarrow S(\text{reg}_n) \leq (1/2 + \varepsilon) n^3$ (by convergence). The chain gives $S(P) \leq S(\text{reg}_n) \leq (1/2+\varepsilon)n^3$. The `constant_ge_half` theorem would follow from the limit: if $S(\text{reg}_n) \geq n^3/2 - n^2$ then $\liminf_{n\to\infty} S(\text{reg}_n)/n^3 \geq 1/2$, combined with the limit existing gives $c \geq 1/2$.
